Predict Means from a Bayesian Scale Model

Source: R/bayes_scale_methods.R
predict.multiScaleR_bayes.Rd

Predict expected responses, or linear predictors, at fitted or new observations. Each prediction carries the joint posterior uncertainty in the scales, the coefficients, and the random effects. A site or year that was not in the fitted data needs an explicit choice, either drawing its effect from the estimated spread among groups or setting it to zero.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_bayes'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  type = c("response", "link"),
  re.form = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  level = 0.95,
  draws = NULL,
  kernel_inputs = NULL,
  row_id = NULL,
  scale_re.form = NULL,
  new_scale_levels = c("error", "sample", "zero"),
  new_response_levels = c("error", "sample", "zero"),
  seed = NULL,
  include_fixed = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A fitted multiScale_bayes() object with posterior draws, from sampling or either approximation.

newdata

NULL (default) uses the fitted observations. Otherwise a nonempty data frame of new observations that holds the fixed covariates, the offset variables, and the grouping variables of every component you include. Response values are neither needed nor used.

type

"response" (default) returns expected responses, which are expected counts for Poisson and NB2 models, success probabilities for binomial models (also for grouped binomial data), and means for Gaussian models. "link" returns the linear predictor.

re.form

NULL (default) includes the response random effects. NA sets them all to zero while keeping group-specific scales. This is a reference prediction, not an average over the random effects.

summary

Logical. TRUE (default) returns posterior summaries. FALSE returns the matrix of draws by observations.

level

Probability of the central interval; default 0.95.

draws

Optional positive integer number of evenly spaced posterior draws to use. The default NULL uses every draw. Fewer draws save time and memory at a cost in simulation precision.

kernel_inputs

Prepared landscape inputs for newdata, from kernel_prep() or kernel_prep_by_group(). Required with new data and NULL otherwise. Use the fitted kernel, predictor definitions, and physical map units. See "Match new rows to their landscapes" in predict.multiScaleR_bayes().

row_id

Name of the column in newdata that matches each row to an entry of kernel_inputs$binned$point_ids, or to a row name of kernel_inputs$kernel_dat for surface-only inputs. IDs may repeat. The default NULL uses the fitted row-ID column when the fit kept it, and the row names of newdata otherwise. Supply it for fits saved by older versions of the package. Used only with new data.

scale_re.form

NULL (default) includes the fitted scale random effects and any sampled new ones. NA sets every scale deviation to zero. It is separate from re.form, which controls response effects.

new_scale_levels, new_response_levels

What to do with a group level that was not in the fitted data, set separately for scale and response random effects. "error" (default) stops, "sample" draws a new effect, and "zero" sets the new effect to zero. A sampled effect is one standard-normal value per new group and posterior draw, multiplied by that draw's group SD, and shared by every row in the group. Zeroing gives a typical-group reference, not a population average. Known groups keep their fitted effects. Neither choice creates a coefficient for a new level of a fixed factor.

seed

Optional positive integer seed for sampled new effects. Your own random-number state is restored afterward, even when prediction fails.

include_fixed

Logical. With new data, TRUE recomputes declared fixed-radius landscape predictors from kernel_inputs, using their original preparation means and SDs. The default FALSE requires those columns in newdata. Source, metric, radius, kernel, and resolution must match the fitted preparation, including its max_D buffer extent. This adds no scale parameters or uncertainty.

...

Not used. Supplying any further argument is an error.

Value

With summary = TRUE, a data frame with one row per observation, in the supplied order.

  • row: the position of the observation.

  • point_id: its prepared landscape ID.

  • mean, median, sd, lower, upper: summaries of the predicted quantity on the scale set by type. lower and upper bound the central level credible interval.

  • new_scale_level, new_response_level (new data only): whether the row belongs to an unseen group of an included scale or response component.

With summary = FALSE, a numeric matrix with one row per posterior draw and one column per observation.

Results for new data carry a new_groups attribute, a data frame with component, covariate, group, level, and action that lists each unseen level and whether it was sampled or set to zero. Summaries also carry a prediction_contract attribute that describes the target, the included effects, the uncertainty, and the stored parameter map (see prediction_contract). Its diagnostic status repeats the fit's own status. Prediction does not make a failed fit eligible.

What the intervals include

Intervals describe uncertainty in the expected response or the linear predictor. They include uncertainty in the scales, the coefficients, and the fitted group effects, and, when new effects are sampled, the variation among new groups. They leave out the scatter of a single new observation around its mean. Use simulate.multiScaleR_bayes() for that. Each interval is marginal for one observation, not a simultaneous band. mean and sd summarize a finite set of draws and do not show that the corresponding moment exists, so prefer the median and the interval limits for long-tailed predictions.

Match new rows to their landscapes

kernel_inputs supplies the prepared bins for the prediction locations and maps. Each prepared location has one unique entry in binned$point_ids, and row_id matches every row of newdata to one of them. Rows can come in any order and can repeat, as for repeated visits to one location. Build the inputs with kernel_prep() or kernel_prep_by_group(), as in vignette("v06-year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR"). Keep the fitted kernel, predictor definitions, and projected map units. The numerical distance normalizer unit_conv may differ and is converted internally, but that does not convert coordinate systems or physical units. Kernel means need bins. Weighted SQ needs matching source and metric specifications and the raw cell buffers.

Prediction reuses the fitted reference center and spread, the contrasts, and the formula bases. It never standardizes the new rows on their own, never learns a new scale reference, and never refits the model or uses responses in newdata. A new kernel uses only the neighborhood you prepared, so a predicted scale larger than max_D cannot draw on cells beyond it.

Choose how to treat new groups

vignette("v14-bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR") compares the choices in a table. A few rules matter for every call. An unseen level of a fixed year factor, such as factor(year), is always an error, under every policy. To predict response years you have not surveyed, use a random intercept for year or a scientifically justified numeric trend. Exchangeable annual effects impose no trend or autocorrelation. predict_scales() can still predict a new year's scale when the response formula has fixed year effects. Setting new effects to zero is not integration over group variation, and with a nonlinear link or kernel the two predictions generally differ. Grouping columns used only by a component you leave out with re.form = NA or scale_re.form = NA may be absent from newdata.

Predict jointly across rows

Put every row whose joint prediction matters into one call. Within a call, all new rows in the same grouping term and level share one new effect for each posterior draw. Distinct terms and groups follow the model's conditional independence, and the joint posterior dependence among parameters is kept. Separate calls draw separate new effects, so do not combine independently generated batches to infer joint spatial or annual uncertainty or a total. For a total of expected values, set summary = FALSE and sum each row of the matrix with rowSums().

The full matrix of draws by observations is built even when summary = TRUE, at 8 bytes per value. When you need only an interval for each location of a large map, predict smaller batches and keep their summaries, or lower draws at a cost in simulation precision.

Use formula transformations safely

scale(), poly(), splines::ns(), and splines::bs() keep their training definitions inside ordinary expressions such as I(scale(temp)) and in transformed offsets, so single rows, batches, and effect curves use the same constants. An expression such as I(x - mean(x)) instead takes its mean from the new batch, by ordinary R formula rules. Compute such a covariate with training constants before fitting when you need the original centering. Transforms must come from base R or stats, or carry an explicit package namespace. Custom functions defined only in the fitting workspace are not saved with the model, so compute them as covariate columns instead. New levels of a fixed factor are always rejected. For fits saved without design metadata, the rebuilt formula must reproduce the stored training matrix from the original data, or prediction stops. Give a namespace prefix to any custom function that reuses a learner name such as scale.

Know what prediction cannot fix

Prediction passes the fitted posterior forward. It does not repair failed sampling, an inaccurate approximation, or a misspecified observation model, and it does not check the fit's diagnostics, so inspect summary(object)$diagnostics first. Every method uses its stored joint draws. For an importance-corrected fit these are resampled candidates, so prediction has the finite precision of those resamples rather than a fresh weighted integration.

Prediction stops on unmatched IDs, new fixed-factor levels, unavailable formula transforms, incompatible kernel inputs, and nonfinite results. It never clips scales to the input limits or replaces a problematic draw.

To test predictions, hold out data at the level you intend to predict. A held-out visit at a known site and year is easier to predict than a whole new site or year, and repeated sites or years are not independent validation replicates. cross_validate_bayes() refits the model without the held-out rows and scores them.

See also

multiScale_bayes(), multiScaleR_bayes, posterior_scales(), prediction_contract, predict_scales(), simulate.multiScaleR_bayes(), cross_validate_bayes(), multiScaleR-prediction for prediction across the package; vignette("v14-bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR").

Examples

example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
fit <- example$fits$pooled
fitted_means <- predict(fit, draws = 100)
head(fitted_means[c("point_id", "median", "lower", "upper")])
#>   point_id    median    lower     upper
#> 1  s1_2021  3.248331 1.679910  4.551568
#> 2  s2_2021  4.039417 2.317309  7.140053
#> 3  s3_2021 15.054402 9.627522 20.920631
#> 4  s4_2021  4.283389 2.053277  6.393943
#> 5  s5_2021  5.032599 3.267581  7.769735
#> 6  s6_2021  4.818284 2.761564  6.980679
# Expected counts at the fitted rows, including fitted site effects.
# The draw limit keeps this demonstration short. Use all draws for
# final summaries.

# New surveys at known site-years reuse their annual maps and group effects
new_surveys <- example$data[1:3, c("site", "year", "site_year")]
predict(fit, new_surveys, kernel_inputs = example$inputs,
  row_id = "site_year", draws = 100)
#>   row point_id      mean    median        sd    lower     upper new_scale_level
#> 1   1  s1_2021  3.207937  3.248331 0.8470514 1.679910  4.551568           FALSE
#> 2   2  s2_2021  4.176684  4.039417 1.1973646 2.317309  7.140053           FALSE
#> 3   3  s3_2021 15.239878 15.054402 3.2055779 9.627522 20.920631           FALSE
#>   new_response_level
#> 1              FALSE
#> 2              FALSE
#> 3              FALSE
# simulate() would add the scatter of individual counts.

# A fit with random year intercepts can predict new sites and years
forecast <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-prediction-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
future <- predict(forecast$fit, forecast$newdata,
  kernel_inputs = forecast$kernel_inputs, row_id = "site_year",
  new_scale_levels = "sample", new_response_levels = "sample",
  draws = 200, seed = 802)
future[c("point_id", "median", "lower", "upper", "new_response_level")]
#>          point_id    median     lower     upper new_response_level
#> 1         s1_2026  2.947675  1.347987  6.703234               TRUE
#> 2         s2_2026 12.196475  6.777054 22.035955               TRUE
#> 3 new_site_A_2026 19.774712  8.500104 46.423083               TRUE
#> 4 new_site_B_2026  4.269301  1.776990  8.776078               TRUE
#> 5         s1_2027  3.298215  1.528912  6.098285               TRUE
#> 6         s2_2027 13.633387  7.175980 29.062856               TRUE
#> 7 new_site_A_2027 22.960803 10.462792 47.634440               TRUE
#> 8 new_site_B_2027  4.550484  1.923561 11.587764               TRUE
attr(future, "new_groups")   # the unseen levels and what was done to them
#>   component covariate group      level action
#> 1     scale   habitat  year       2026 sample
#> 2     scale   habitat  year       2027 sample
#> 3  response            site new_site_A sample
#> 4  response            site new_site_B sample
#> 5  response            year       2026 sample
#> 6  response            year       2027 sample
